opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, and I don't think long-horizon coherence is the last piece. Even if a model can stay on task for hours or days, a few things could still hold it back.

One is what you might call taste or judgment: knowing which problems are worth working on and which approaches are promising. Humans who are really good at research or engineering have a sense of what's going to pan out, and it comes from years of feedback on whether their bets paid off. It's not obvious we'll get that just by extending the horizon of RL. The reward signals for "was this a good research direction" are sparse and delayed, so they're hard to train on.

Another is sample efficiency, meaning how quickly the model learns from its own experience in a new setting. When a person joins a new company or codebase, they're pretty useless for a while, and then they pick up the local context. If models can't do that kind of in-context or online learning well, you'll have this awkward situation where they're very capable in general but brittle on the specifics of your environment.

Then there are the more mundane issues of multimodality and interacting with real software and the physical world. A lot of real work involves clicking around in messy interfaces, reading screens, dealing with tools that weren't designed for an AI. I expect those to get solved, but they could be a drag for a while.

Finally there's error recovery. Over a long trajectory, small mistakes compound. The model needs to notice when it's gone off the rails and backtrack, rather than confidently continuing down a wrong path. Some of that should come from long-horizon RL itself, but how robust it gets is still an open question.

So my guess is that once coherence over long horizons is solved, you'd see a big jump in usefulness. But you'd probably still find the models somewhat uneven: superhuman in some areas, surprisingly weak in others, and the weak spots would mostly be about judgment and adapting to new contexts.

r001.rationale: It says models may lack the taste or judgment that helps human research and engineering experts choose promising problems and approaches.

r002.rationale: It does not identify difficulty handling ambiguity as a remaining gap between AI models and human experts.

r003.rationale: It describes interface and environment interaction as a drag “for a while” and says those issues are expected to be solved.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing people sometimes assume is that once you've got long-horizon RL working, and the model can stay coherent over a day or a week of work, then you've basically solved the problem and everything else is downstream of that. And I don't think that's quite right. I think there are a few things that remain.

One is sample efficiency. Right now, the way we train these models, they see enormous amounts of data compared to what a person sees. And when you move to long-horizon tasks, that gets worse, not better, because each episode is long and expensive and the reward signal is sparse. So you end up in this regime where the model might be able to execute a long task, but learning a new skill on the job, from a handful of examples, is still something it does worse than a person would. Humans are extremely good at learning from very little experience, and I think a lot of that comes from the prior we have, but some of it is a genuine difference in how learning works. So I'd expect that to be a bottleneck for a while, especially for things that are niche enough that there's not a lot of relevant data.

Another one is what I'd call the feedback problem. For a lot of the tasks we actually care about, there isn't a clean reward you can compute. Writing code, you can run tests, and that's why coding has been the first domain where this stuff really takes off. But a lot of real work is more like, "was this a good decision?" and you only find out six months later, or you never find out. And if the model is operating for a long time without any ground truth, it needs some pretty good internal sense of whether it's on the right track. Humans have taste, and I think the models have some of that too, but it's much less well developed, and it's not obvious long-horizon RL on verifiable tasks gives it to you for free.

There's also the question of the model's own self-knowledge. If it's going to work on something for a week, it needs to know what it doesn't know, when to stop and ask, when to go look something up, when to be uncertain. Models are still fairly bad at that. They'll confidently proceed on a wrong premise. Over a short task that costs you a few minutes. Over a long task it can mean the whole thing is wasted.

And then the last thing, which is maybe more mundane but I think matters a lot, is just the environment. The model has to interact with the world through some set of tools and interfaces, and a lot of the friction in real work is institutional. Getting access to things, understanding how an organization actually works, dealing with the fact that the documentation is wrong. Some of that gets solved by building better scaffolding, but some of it is just slow, in the sense that the world has to adapt to having these agents around, and that takes time regardless of how good the model is.

So I'd say, long-horizon RL is a big unlock, but I'd expect the models to still be uneven. Really strong at some things, surprisingly weak at others, and the weak spots will be the things where there's no good feedback signal and the model has to rely on judgment it hasn't really been trained to have.

r001.rationale: The candidate says humans have taste and models have a less developed version, making judgment a remaining weakness.

r002.rationale: It describes models’ uncertainty and self-knowledge problems, but does not identify a gap in handling ambiguity compared with human experts.

r003.rationale: The candidate says some friction may be addressed with better scaffolding, but that institutional barriers and adaptation can take time; it does not suggest these barriers are likely to be short-lived.

astra-6.text:
I think long-horizon coherence would remove an important bottleneck, but it wouldn’t necessarily remove the bottleneck of knowing what to do. You could have a model that works very consistently toward a goal for a week, but gets stuck because it’s missing some conceptual insight. Working for longer helps if the problem can be decomposed into steps the model already knows how to do. It’s less clear how much it helps when you need a fundamentally new idea.

Then there’s the question of feedback. For some tasks, you can try something and quickly tell whether it worked. For others, you might have to run an experiment, or wait for something to happen in the world. Even if the model can think much faster, that loop could still be slow. And during training, you need some way to reward progress without rewarding things that merely look like progress.

So I’d distinguish being able to keep working from being able to make productive progress. I’d expect longer-horizon reinforcement learning to help with both, but I wouldn’t assume that solving the first automatically solves the second.

r001.rationale: The response discusses missing conceptual insight but does not identify a gap in taste between AI models and human experts.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention ambiguity handling or compare AI models with human experts.

r003.rationale: The response discusses slow feedback loops, but does not say that interface or environment-access barriers are likely to be short-lived.

sol-6.1.text:
I think exploration could still be a pretty big bottleneck. Being able to work coherently for a long time doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll discover the right approach. You might just spend a long time pursuing something that doesn’t work.

For tasks where you can check the answer, you can train on lots of attempts and reinforce the successful ones. But if success is extremely rare, you may never get the signal you need. So there’s a question of how you get a curriculum that takes you from things the model can already do to genuinely new capabilities.

And then there’s the question of feedback. For some kinds of research or engineering, finding out whether an idea is good requires running an experiment, or waiting for something to happen in the world. Even if the model can think much faster, that part might not speed up very much.

So I wouldn’t assume that solving long-horizon coherence automatically solves everything else. It would let us see much more clearly which limitations are about maintaining a plan, and which are about coming up with a good plan in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response discusses exploration and choosing a good plan, but does not identify a gap in taste between AI models and human experts.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention ambiguity or a model-versus-expert gap in handling it.

r003.rationale: It notes that real-world experiments and feedback may not speed up, but does not say limitations from model interfaces or environmental access are likely to be short-lived.
